primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7223136/ (Poster P169, spontaneous physical activity in sarcopenic older women)
assessment: Thirty-two women were randomized to resistance training plus fish oil or resistance training plus sunflower-oil capsules. The outcomes were activity-monitor steps and sedentary time, with no swallowing assessment. The same poster appears in the companion meeting volume.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7223455/ (Poster P169, spontaneous physical activity in sarcopenic older women)
assessment: This second copy of poster P169 describes the same 32-woman exercise study and sunflower-oil placebo. It duplicates the companion proceedings report and gives no refined-sunflower-oil swallowing result.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10035755/ (Methods 2.1–2.3, listeners, exclusions and speech-in-noise threshold)
assessment: The experiment measures recognition of target words by listeners in background noise. The authors exclude the two participants who reported Parkinson disease from analysis and administer no lemon balm.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10585969/ (Second-thalamotomy results and Supplementary Table S2)
assessment: Speakers with essential tremor were evaluated after staged ultrasound thalamotomy. Frenchay Dysarthria Assessment speech intelligibility scores did not change at group level after the second procedure, and no fresh lemon balm was studied.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10733367/ (Methods, participant groups and acoustic speech tasks)
assessment: The study compares acoustic features across Parkinson disease, frontotemporal dementia and controls, including sustained phonation. The data concern disease-related features and methodological handling of MFCCs, without a lemon balm intervention.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12261282/ (Treatment by etiology, topical vitamin A benefit and harms)
assessment: The olfaction consensus lists peanut oil as a possible topical vitamin A additive and warns about peanut allergy. The cited therapeutic comparison concerns vitamin A and does not isolate refined dietary peanut oil.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12753417/ (Stilbenes subsection and discussion of dietary fats)
assessment: Peanuts are named as a food containing stilbenes, and peanut oil is one dietary source of monounsaturated fats. These are composition or broad diet contexts without a tested refined peanut oil and olfactory outcome.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13741781/ (Olfactory preference test methods and post-traumatic results)
assessment: Peanut oil carried peanut butter in the attractive test odor given to mice after mild traumatic brain injury. The comparison evaluates injury-associated odor preference and does not isolate peanut oil from peanut butter or test dietary refined oil.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4848655/ (Whole dietary patterns in aging and n-3 PUFA clinical study overview)
assessment: The review cites extra-virgin olive oil in relation to cognition. Patients with acute ischemic stroke and dysphagia appear in a separate study of n-3 supplementation and inflammatory markers.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6979458/ (ALS clinical overview; Mediterranean Diet and Extra-Virgin Olive Oil)
assessment: The dysphagia context is progressive ALS. In a separate oxidative-stress section, EVOO is discussed for PREDIMED cognition and proposed neuroprotection without a swallowing effect estimate.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6986528/ (Levodopa effects, formulation table and rabbit pharmacokinetic results)
assessment: Olive oil is the vehicle in an intranasal levodopa suspension compared with other levodopa formulations in rabbits. Dysphagia is mentioned among clinical levodopa symptoms in the introduction, not measured as a dietary oil result.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7278852/ (Patient-reported diet study and Parkinson eating barriers)
assessment: The review cites olive oil within a set of dietary habits associated with broader Parkinson severity. It discusses dysphagia as a source of altered dietary choices, without separately testing whether EVOO affects it.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8127090/ (Gastroesophageal reflux symptoms and dietary approaches)
assessment: Dysphagia is described in reflux and as a warning symptom in the assessment. Olive oil is a constituent of an eating pattern discussed for GERD occurrence, without a swallowing-severity comparison by oil.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12146881/ (Nutrition section on Mediterranean diets and stroke section on dysphagia)
assessment: The statistics report cites extra-virgin olive oil within Mediterranean-diet trials measuring metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes. Poststroke dysphagia appears in the stroke discussion and is not an oil trial endpoint.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11927060/ (Huntington gastrointestinal manifestations and Mediterranean diet section)
assessment: Dysphagia is described as a Huntington disease symptom. EVOO appears in the composition of a Mediterranean pattern in a separate diet discussion without an oil-specific swallowing result.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11068646/ (Bowel and dysphagia symptoms discussion and olive polyphenol section)
assessment: Dysphagia is discussed in the clinical context of Lewy body dementia. The olive-oil polyphenols hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein aglycone are discussed for locomotion in an alpha-synuclein model, not a clinical swallowing outcome.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11137262/ (Parkinson gastrointestinal manifestations and Mediterranean/MIND dietary patterns)
assessment: Dysphagia is a symptom discussed alongside other gastrointestinal manifestations. Olive oil is listed in whole dietary patterns, with no isolated dietary oil or swallowing-severity comparison.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11520510/ (Characteristics of studies, Rusch 2021 and separate Parkinson constipation trial eligibility)
assessment: One trial entry describes using olive oil within a prescribed Mediterranean diet and targets bowel function. Elsewhere dysphagia is mentioned in eligibility for a separate constipation study. The review gives no swallowing outcome contrasting isolated oil.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12256702/ (Nutrition section on Mediterranean diets and stroke section on dysphagia)
assessment: The 2025 statistics update reviews olive-oil-related cardiovascular outcomes and separately summarizes poststroke dysphagia prevalence and prognosis. It provides no independent dietary oil comparison for swallowing difficulty.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12087861/ (Later-life microbiota section; diet and older-adult interventions)
assessment: Impaired swallowing reflex is discussed as an age-related contributor to nutrition changes. Olive oil is a constituent of a Mediterranean dietary intervention reviewed for microbiome and healthy-aging outcomes.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12292727/ (Clinical motor manifestations and dietary polyphenols)
assessment: The paper lists dysphagia among clinical Parkinson manifestations and includes extra-virgin olive oil in sources of polyphenols. The reviewed mechanism and probiotic or dietary findings provide no isolated oil swallowing outcome.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12897292/ (Mediterranean Dietary Patterns and Challenges in Dietary Intake)
assessment: Dysphagia is discussed as a contributor to advanced Parkinson malnutrition and altered diet. Olive oil is named in the description of Mediterranean diet composition without a dietary swallowing comparison.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13516459/ (Non-motor symptoms and dietary survey discussion)
assessment: The overview describes Parkinson dysphagia and aspiration risk. Its cited food-frequency study links several foods including olive oil with overall Parkinson progression without an EVOO-specific swallowing result in this report.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12704985/ (Experiment 1 stimulus sentences and task methods; Experiment 2 perception methods)
assessment: The Parkinson speech study tests production and recognition of contrastive stress in elicited and repeated Mandarin sentences. Listener accuracy is task based and participants were not assigned watermelon consumption.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10733367/ (Methods, acoustic features and clinical participant groups)
assessment: The comparisons are based on speech recordings and MFCC measurements across clinical groups and control speakers. Neither ground caraway intake nor its effect on intelligibility is a variable.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7707995/ (Clinical ALS characteristics and Terpenoids subsection)
assessment: Dysphagia is described in late ALS, while Asparagus adscendens root extract appears in a scopolamine amnesia animal study. An extract from a different species and plant part does not give a steamed food swallowing result.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11040388/ (Clinical manifestations of brain tumors and Quercetin subsection)
assessment: Asparagus appears as one of several food sources of quercetin. Dysphagia is mentioned among manifestations of brain tumors, without a steamed-asparagus intervention or swallowing comparison.
